body:
A Gupta inscription on an Ashokan pillar

The Allahabad Pillar Inscription, also known as the Prayaga Prashasti, is an important source for the reign of Samudragupta of the Gupta dynasty in the 4th century CE.

The pillar is associated with Prayaga, the historical name of the area now known as Prayagraj, formerly Allahabad, in Uttar Pradesh. It is particularly important because the Gupta inscription was engraved on a pillar that also bears inscriptions of the earlier Mauryan emperor Ashoka.

Thus, the physical pillar is associated with Ashoka, but the famous Prayaga Prashasti praises Samudragupta. These are not the same inscriptions.

Language, script and composer

The Prayaga Prashasti was composed in Sanskrit by Harishena, also written Harisena, who was a poet and important official at Samudragupta's court.

Its script is a Gupta-period variety of Brahmi, described more specifically as an eastern form of the Gupta alphabet. The inscription is generally dated to the middle of the 4th century CE.

The term prashasti means a composition of praise. Harishena presents Samudragupta as a powerful warrior, an accomplished ruler and a person possessing admirable qualities.

What does the inscription record?

The inscription is especially important for understanding Samudragupta's military campaigns and his different policies towards defeated rulers.

Rulers of Aryavarta

Aryavarta refers here to the northern Indian region described in the inscription. The prashasti records the defeat of 9 rulers of Aryavarta. Their kingdoms were incorporated into Samudragupta's expanding empire.

Rulers of Dakshinapatha

Dakshinapatha refers to the southern region. The inscription describes the defeat of 12 rulers of Dakshinapatha. Samudragupta defeated these rulers but subsequently allowed them to resume ruling their kingdoms while accepting his authority.

This distinction is more important than simply memorising that Samudragupta fought campaigns in both regions.

Frontier and distant rulers

The prashasti also refers to neighbouring states and groups that acknowledged Samudragupta's authority by bringing tribute, obeying commands or attending his court. It further describes relations with rulers of more distant regions.

These passages show that Samudragupta's political influence was not expressed everywhere through direct annexation. Different rulers could have different relationships with the Gupta emperor.

Distinguish Harishena and Ravikirti

Harishena composed the Sanskrit Prayaga Prashasti praising Samudragupta. Ravikirti composed the Sanskrit Aihole inscription praising Pulakeshin II. Both are associated with royal prashastis, but they belong to different rulers, dynasties, places and centuries.

Prelims focus

  • Allahabad Pillar Inscription is also called the Prayaga Prashasti.
  • It praises Samudragupta of the Gupta dynasty, in the 4th century CE.
  • Composer: Harishena. Language: Sanskrit. Script: Gupta-period Brahmi.
  • 9 Aryavarta rulers were defeated and their kingdoms incorporated.
  • 12 Dakshinapatha rulers were defeated and allowed to rule again.
  • Trap: The pillar is associated with Ashoka, but the Prayaga Prashasti praises Samudragupta.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – I, Class 6, Ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed pp. 111–114; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Ch. 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 36–37; GCERT, History, Standard 11, Ch. 9, 'India During the Gupta Period', printed p. 56; Archaeological Survey of India, BharatSHRI, 'Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Samudragupta', consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Samudragupta incorporated the kingdoms of 9 Aryavarta rulers; 12 Dakshinapatha rulers resumed ruling under his superior position.
pictures.caption: Samudragupta's inscription describes different treatment of northern and southern rulers.

title: Allahabad Pillar Inscription: Samudragupta's Prayaga Prashasti

body:
The inscription at Aihole

The Aihole inscription is associated with the Meguti Jain temple at Aihole in present-day Karnataka. It is a major source for the reign of Pulakeshin II, an important ruler of the Chalukyas of Badami, also called the Western Chalukyas.

The inscription is dated Saka year 556, corresponding to approximately 634–635 CE. It therefore belongs to the 7th century CE, much later than the Mauryan, Shaka and early Gupta inscriptions discussed earlier.

The inscription was composed by Ravikirti, a poet associated with Pulakeshin II's court. Ravikirti also records the construction of the Jain temple. The inscription is a prashasti celebrating the Chalukya ruler's achievements.

Language and script

The main inscription is composed in the Sanskrit language. Its letters belong to an early southern Brahmi-derived script, commonly described as early Kannada or Old Kannada script.

These 2 facts must be kept separate. The script is associated with the early development of Kannada writing, but the language of Ravikirti's prashasti is Sanskrit, not Kannada.

What does the inscription record?

Ravikirti praises Pulakeshin II's military victories and political achievements. For objective examinations, the most important episode is the conflict between Pulakeshin II and the northern ruler Harshavardhana.

Pulakeshin II and Harsha

Harshavardhana was a major ruler of northern India. When he attempted to extend his power towards the Deccan, he encountered opposition from Pulakeshin II. The inscription celebrates Pulakeshin II for checking Harsha's advance, commonly associated with the region of the Narmada River.

In this conflict, Harsha was the ruler whose expansion was stopped, while Pulakeshin II was the Chalukya ruler credited with stopping him. This identifies the correct roles of the 2 rulers.

Conflict with the Pallavas

The prashasti also refers to Pulakeshin II's campaigns against the Pallavas, whose important centre was Kanchipuram in present-day Tamil Nadu.

The Chalukyas and Pallavas were rival powers in the Deccan and southern India. Ravikirti's praise of Pulakeshin II includes his success against the Pallava ruler. The inscription is therefore associated with both the northern conflict involving Harsha and the southern rivalry with the Pallavas.

The importance of the Meguti temple

The inscription is engraved on a stone slab associated with the Meguti Jain temple. The surviving temple provides a direct connection between the inscription, the place where it was recorded and the Chalukya period.

Aihole is in Karnataka, not Gujarat. Its significance here is as an important comparison with the Girnar and Prayaga inscriptions: it is another Sanskrit royal prashasti, but it belongs to a different dynasty, location, century and form of Brahmi-derived script.

Prelims focus

  • Aihole is in Karnataka; the inscription is associated with the Meguti Jain temple.
  • It praises Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas of Badami.
  • Composer: Ravikirti.
  • Date: Saka year 556, approximately 634–635 CE.
  • Language: Sanskrit. Script: early Kannada or southern Brahmi-derived script.
  • Trap: The inscription celebrates Pulakeshin II for checking Harsha's advance, not Harsha for defeating Pulakeshin II.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – I, Class 6, Ch. 11, 'New Empires and Kingdoms', printed pp. 115–116; Archaeological Survey of India, Dharwad Circle, Aihole Museum, English brochure, section on the Meguti Jain temple and Ravikirti inscription, consulted 19 November 2026; F. Kielhorn, 'Aihole Inscription of Pulikesin II, Saka-Samvat 556', Epigraphia Indica, Vol. VI (1900–01), pp. 1–12.]

pictures.caption: The Aihole inscription belongs to the 7th-century Chalukya period and is associated with the Meguti Jain temple.

title: Aihole Inscription: Pulakeshin II and the Chalukyas of Badami

body:
The essential identification table

Ancient Indian inscriptions can be distinguished by 5 closely connected facts: location, ruler, date, language and script, and subject. A question may provide any 2 or 3 of these details and ask the learner to identify the remaining one.

The following table brings together the important inscriptions covered in this lesson.

Inscription and placeRuler and periodLanguage and scriptMain subject
Ashoka's Girnar rock edicts, Junagadh, GujaratAshoka, Maurya; 3rd century BCEPrakrit; BrahmiDhamma, royal instructions, welfare and Kalinga remorse
Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription, GujaratRudradaman I, Western Kshatrapa; 150 CESanskrit; BrahmiRepair of Sudarshana Lake after storm damage
Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription, GujaratSkandagupta, Gupta; 5th century CESanskrit; Gupta-period BrahmiLater repair of Sudarshana Lake after flooding
Prayaga Prashasti, Allahabad pillar, Uttar PradeshSamudragupta, Gupta; 4th century CESanskrit; Gupta-period BrahmiRoyal praise, conquests and treatment of defeated rulers
Aihole inscription, Meguti Jain temple, KarnatakaPulakeshin II, Chalukya; 634–635 CESanskrit; early Kannada scriptRoyal praise, checking Harsha and campaigns against Pallavas

How to distinguish the physical inscription sites

The 5 records do not correspond to 5 separate places. Three rulers are associated with the same Girnar rock: Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta. The other 2 important records are associated with a pillar at Prayaga and a temple at Aihole.

Chronology from the Mauryas to the Chalukyas

The order of the inscriptions also helps identify their rulers. The Mauryan record of Ashoka belongs to the 3rd century BCE. The Shaka record of Rudradaman follows in the 2nd century CE. The Gupta ruler Samudragupta belongs to the 4th century CE, while the Gupta ruler Skandagupta belongs to the 5th century CE. The Chalukya record at Aihole follows in the 7th century CE.

Thus, Samudragupta's Allahabad inscription is chronologically earlier than Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription, even though both rulers belong to the Gupta dynasty.

Three distinctions that prevent common errors

Girnar and Junagadh are not 2 separate inscription sites

Both names refer to the rock-inscription site at the foot of Mount Girnar near Junagadh. The site preserves records of 3 rulers from different dynasties. The subject of an inscription must therefore be matched with its particular ruler, not merely with the location.

Construction and repair of Sudarshana Lake were different events

Pushyagupta originally constructed the lake under Chandragupta Maurya. Tushaspha improved its water channels under Ashoka. Suvishakha carried out the repair associated with Rudradaman I. The later Gupta-period repair was supervised by Chakrapalita during Skandagupta's reign.

Consequently, the statement that Rudradaman built Sudarshana Lake for the first time is incorrect. The more precise statement is that Rudradaman restored a reservoir that already existed.

Harishena and Ravikirti wrote about different rulers

The composer of the Prayaga Prashasti was Harishena, who praised Samudragupta. The composer of the Aihole inscription was Ravikirti, who praised Pulakeshin II.

Both compositions use Sanskrit and praise a powerful ruler, but one belongs to the Gupta Empire of the 4th century CE and the other to the Chalukyas of the 7th century CE.

Prelims focus

  • Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta are associated with the Girnar rock at Junagadh.
  • The Girnar Ashokan edicts are in Prakrit; the later Rudradaman and Skandagupta records are in Sanskrit.
  • Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription: Saka year 72, approximately 150 CE.
  • Samudragupta's Prayaga Prashasti: Harishena, Sanskrit, 4th century CE.
  • Pulakeshin II's Aihole inscription: Ravikirti, Sanskrit, 634–635 CE.
  • Trap: The same script, language or location does not necessarily indicate the same ruler or historical event.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – I, Class 6, Ch. 8, printed pp. 75–81, and Ch. 11, printed pp. 111–116; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Ch. 2, printed pp. 28–38; Archaeological Survey of India, BharatSHRI, entries on the Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman and Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Samudragupta, consulted 19 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Dharwad Circle, Aihole Museum, English brochure, section on the Meguti Jain temple, consulted 19 November 2026; Shubhra Pramanik, 'Significant Discoveries around Sudarshan Lake, Junagadh', Puratattva, Vol. 35 (2004–05), p. 179.]
